stories.headline: NHL season preview: Strengths, weaknesses, X factors for all 32 teams
stories.summary: Will Carolina win the Cup yet again? Who are the top challengers? Get key intel on every club here.
stories.body:
Opening night of the 2026-27 NHL season is Tuesday, which includes a tripleheader of games on ESPN: Florida Panthers-Carolina Hurricanes at 5 p.m. ET (including the Stanley Cup banner-raising), New York Rangers-Boston Bruins at 8 p.m. ET, and Chicago Blackhawks-Vegas Golden Knights at 10:30 p.m. ET.

Before the puck drops, this preview will serve you all the key intel you need on all 32 teams, including strengths, weaknesses, X factors, most likely award winners, fantasy tips and a bold prediction.

This season preview also features the first edition of ESPN's NHL Power Rankings, which provide the order in which these teams are presented. The weekly rankings are formulated through votes from ESPN hockey broadcasters, analysts and reporters.

Note: Thanks to PuckPedia for salary and contract data. Advanced stats are from Hockey Reference, Natural Stat Trick and Evolving Hockey. Kristen Shilton profiled the teams in the Eastern Conference, while Ryan S. Clark handled the Western Conference clubs. The fantasy outlook for each team was written by Victoria Matiash and Sean Allen, and bold predictions are from Greg Wyshynski. Stanley Cup odds are courtesy of DraftKings as of Sept. 26 and are subject to change. Projected points are via Stathletes.

1. Carolina Hurricanes
Last season: 53-22-7 (113 points), won the Stanley Cup

Stanley Cup odds: +650

Projected points: 112.2

Biggest strength: The Hurricanes are stacked with top forwards and enviable depth performers. It's the combination that made Carolina champions four months ago, and versatility will be a trademark for this group again. Star skaters like Andrei Svechnikov (coming off a rebound season), Sebastian Aho (a puck-moving playmaker), Nikolaj Ehlers, Taylor Hall, Jordan Staal, Jackson Blake -- there's no shortage of showstoppers for coach Rod Brind'Amour to use in formulating the Hurricanes' attack up front. And Carolina's back end (not to mention its perennially excellent penalty kill) is powered by the heart and soul of Jaccob Slavin ahead of a strong supporting cast (including his partner Jalen Chatfield and K'Andre Miller). Carolina's reputation is built on good defensive habits, strong special teams and enough firepower to give it a consistent edge over the competition. That steadiness will be essential in the Hurricanes' hunt for another title.

Biggest concern: Carolina didn't make many adjustments to the roster over the summer, with one notable exception: GM Eric Tulsky let starting goaltender Frederik Andersen walk in free agency, officially handing the crease over to Brandon Bussi and Pyotr Kochetkov. After Bussi replaced Andersen late in Carolina's Cup run last spring, it's not entirely surprising the 28-year-old is getting a shot at being the No. 1 moving forward. But Bussi's short résumé -- he jumped into the NHL a year ago -- could be a liability, particularly considering Carolina no longer has a veteran in the wings to support him. And strong goaltending will be imperative for the Hurricanes early on when scoring itself might be at a higher premium, as Seth Jarvis will be notably unavailable to start the year as he recovers from offseason surgery. Carolina won't have the still-unsigned Alexander Nikishin patrolling the blue line to shield Bussi, either. The goaltender will have to show quickly that his magic touch still remains to keep Carolina on course.

This season hinges on ... how well Carolina handles the dreaded Stanley Cup hangover. It's a real thing. The Hurricanes wouldn't be the first champions to feel lethargic following a summer of celebration. There are renewed expectations and pressure to be dominant out of the gate with the opportunity to be repeat contenders -- a tall task even if Carolina were fully healthy and with the ink dried on every outstanding contract. The first few weeks of the year will be critical for the Hurricanes to reestablish their identity as a hungry team still looking to prove itself despite how well last spring ended.

Most likely award winner: Jaccob Slavin, Lady Byng Trophy

Fantasy outlook: Carolina's relentless system floats everyone's floor, with Sebastian Aho, Andrei Svechnikov and Nikolaj Ehlers as the weapons. A healthy Shayne Gostisbehere is the power-play bet, as he was 22nd in assists per minute in just 55 games, so the helpers spike if he stays on the ice. -- Allen

Bold prediction: Jordan Staal wins the Selke Trophy. -- Wyshynski

2. Colorado Avalanche
Last season: 55-16-11 (121 points), lost in conference finals

Stanley Cup odds: +700

Projected points: 115.7

Biggest strength: The Avs have two of the five best players in the world in Nathan MacKinnon and Cale Makar. And while true, the Avalanche also possess what is expected to be one of the most complete teams in the NHL. The group returns 17 players from last year's roster, which won the Presidents' Trophy for the best regular-season record, and reached the conference finals; this summer, they added Stanley Cup winner Jaden Schwartz. The Avs have shown they can receive goals from every part of their lineup, have a defensive structure that involves contributions from every skater, and they have a goalie tandem that has become one of the best in the league.

Biggest concern: In terms of the regular season? It's seeing how young players such as Gavin Brindley, Zachary L'Heureux, Fedor Svechkov and T.J. Hughes find roles with the team. Brindley was on the roster last season, while Hughes joined the AHL club after finishing his season at Michigan, while the latter two were acquired in the offseason. All could potentially make a difference. Not only because they'd give the Avs even more depth, but they'd be doing it at a relatively cheap price for a team that has a little more than $400,000 in salary cap space. And if depth development isn't the biggest concern, it's finding a solution for a power play that was the sixth worst in the NHL last season.

This season hinges on ... correcting what went wrong in the playoffs. Losing in the conference finals to the Golden Knights created questions about how the Avs went from having the NHL's most dangerous attack to one that sputtered at the end. The Avs are one of the teams that won't be judged on what they do through 84 games, but rather the 16 games they must win in their pursuit of another title.

Most likely award winner: Cale Makar, Norris Trophy

Fantasy outlook: Martin Necas accumulated 100 points riding shotgun to Nathan MacKinnon in 2025-26. No reason to expect any different this round. Lower down the fantasy ranks, Gabriel Landeskog sports greater potential, now that the captain feels good and up to speed, especially competing on the top power play. -- Matiash

Bold prediction: Avalanche win the Western Conference. -- Wyshynski

3. Dallas Stars
Last season: 50-20-12 (112 points), lost in first round

Stanley Cup odds: +1400

Projected points: 101.7

Biggest strength: Once again, it appears the Stars have everything needed to present a serious case to win the Stanley Cup. They return 20 players from last year's team that had the No. 2 power play and was in the top 10 in goals per game while having nine players who finished with 10 or more goals. Their defensive structure was among the best in the NHL when it came to allowing the fewest high-danger chances per 60, scoring chances per 60 and shots per 60. Plus, their goaltending was also in the top 10 in team save percentage in 5-on-5 play.

Biggest concern: Can everyone stay healthy? Jamie Benn, Matt Duchene, Radek Faksa, Roope Hintz, Mikko Rantanen and Tyler Seguin all played fewer than 70 games last season. One way to look at those absences is it's six forwards who serve in numerous roles. Another way to view it is that the Stars were essentially without two lines and had to tap into their depth. Going through another season of that could be challenging for a team that has less than $400,000 in salary cap space to start the season.

This season hinges on ... identifying the disconnect that led to them getting knocked out in the first round after reaching three consecutive conference finals. Injuries played a role, and those challenges carried over into the playoffs. But so were the struggles the Stars faced when it came to scoring and defending. They were eliminated in the first round, averaging 2.50 goals per game while allowing 3.83 per contest, the latter of which was the second highest in the playoffs.

Most likely award winner: Jason Robertson, Rocket Richard

Fantasy outlook: Slipping through the cracks in fantasy a bit, Miro Heiskanen remains a top-10 defenseman with such a solid group of dynamite skaters. If healthy, Jake Oettinger is going to play, and win, enough to merit rostering as a No. 1 goalie. -- Matiash

Bold prediction: Stars hit the John Tortorella panic button in-season. -- Wyshynski

4. Florida Panthers
Last season: 40-38-4 (84 points), missed playoffs

Stanley Cup odds: +650

Projected points: 102.6

Biggest strength: Is Florida's lineup big enough for two Tkachuk brothers? The answer is, well, probably yes. Prepare for the Brady and Matthew Show to highlight the Panthers' offense now in complement to elite talents such as Aleksander Barkov and Sam Reinhart. On paper, this Florida pack should be a potent top-six unit. Barkov's return after missing all of last season is a shot in the arm for Florida at even strength and on the power play -- he's an incomparable two-way threat after all -- and having Brady on his wing allows Barkov to expand further as a playmaker. Paul Maurice constantly finds ways to push the right buttons for his team, and Florida can hang its hat on what it does well, possessing the puck with a verifiably star-studded offensive front.

Biggest concern: Florida is going from Sergei Bobrovsky to Jacob Markstrom in the starter's net, and that feels like a possible red flag. Bobrovsky was admittedly poor last season -- producing his worst numbers in over a decade -- but he's a two-time Vezina winner who guided Florida to a pair of Stanley Cup championships in the last five years. Markstrom, on the other hand, is something of a wild card. He was at his best statistically five years ago in Calgary (earning a Vezina nomination in 2022) but never found a consistent game from there for the Flames or through two seasons in New Jersey. Is Florida the fresh start Markstrom needs to reemerge as an elite-caliber goaltender? And can Akira Schmid -- the Panthers' new backup -- provide Markstrom with the right partner to help Florida pick up where it left off two seasons ago as a playoff contender? It's fair to wonder.

This season hinges on ... health and depth. The devastating loss of Barkov to an ACL injury before last season began was a gut punch to Florida's operation. Ensuring Barkov is back at full strength -- and going full speed -- is what breathes life back into the Panthers' offense (they ranked 18th there without him, averaging 3.00 goals per game). Matthew Tkachuk's limited showing -- at just 31 games -- hurt as well. Their availability is a massive advantage for Florida -- but especially critical given the Panthers' depth concerns early on. Brad Marchand will be sidelined through October following surgery, and Jonah Gadjovich still isn't back from his own procedure in November 2025. The Panthers lost significant secondary threats in the offseason -- like Evan Rodrigues, A.J. Greer and Mackie Samoskevich -- without necessarily filling in all those holes.

Most likely award winner: Aleksander Barkov, Selke Trophy

Fantasy outlook: A down fantasy year sets up a roaring return, with both Brady and Matthew Tkachuk now up front and a healthy Aleksander Barkov back. Brad Marchand is the ageless draft pick -- fourth in the entire league in goals per minute at age 38, available at a discount because he played only 52 games. -- Allen

Bold prediction: Panthers win the Stanley Cup. -- Wyshynski

5. Vegas Golden Knights
Last season: 39-26-17 (95 points), lost in Stanley Cup Final

Stanley Cup odds: +850

Projected points: 106.9

Biggest strength: The Golden Knights return 16 players from the roster that advanced to the Stanley Cup Final, enough to suggest they are in an enviable place. They are among the quartet of teams that control the Western Conference going back to 2020, based on the core they've built and how they've added to that collective. Possessing that level of continuity could also be extremely beneficial as first-year head coach Ryan Craig takes over. Craig is a former Golden Knights assistant who was promoted after coaching the franchise's AHL team since 2023.

Biggest concern: There are a few to choose from, whether it's how a first-time NHL head coach navigates a Stanley Cup front-runner, to what they do to fill the void left by trading away last year's leading goal scorer, Pavel Dorofeyev. Yet the primary answer could be the goaltending. The Golden Knights encountered a few challenges in the regular season when it came to how they operated in net. Inconsistencies and injuries led to them using four different goalies, while their team save percentage was the NHL's second lowest in 5-on-5 play.

This season hinges on ... their goaltending. The Golden Knights' play in the defensive zone last season is what made the dynamics around their goalies even more puzzling. They allowed the fewest high-danger chances per 60, the second-fewest shots per 60 and the fourth-fewest scoring chances per 60. Identifying what led to the Golden Knights having one of the worst team save percentages last season -- and addressing that issue -- could play a role in Craig having one of the strongest seasons by a first-year coach in recent memory.

Most likely award winner: Jack Eichel, Hart Trophy

Fantasy outlook: What should fantasy managers make of Carter Hart's potential this year? After a whole year off due to his legal situation, the netminder was more than just reliable for a Golden Knights team that made it all the way to the Stanley Cup Final. But he played only 40 games total between the regular and postseason. There are other starting netminders, for other good squads, who carry less uncertainty. -- Matiash

Bold prediction: Mitch Marner scores 100 points. -- Wyshynski

6. Minnesota Wild
Last season: 46-24-12 (104 points), lost in second round

Stanley Cup odds: +1300

Projected points: 97.4

Biggest strength: The discussion around the Wild has changed because of what they did last season. They've gone from being a team that heavily relied on its defensive identity to fight for a wild-card spot to one that finished with more than 100 points while presenting a case that they could challenge the power dynamic in the Western Conference. Having a star quartet featuring Matt Boldy, Brock Faber, Quinn Hughes and Kirill Kaprizov was vital, and Minnesota finished the regular season averaging the 11th-most goals per game while allowing the fourth-fewest goals per game.

Biggest concern: There might have been an overreliance on the goalie tandem of Filip Gustavsson and Jesper Wallstedt. Gustavsson and Wallstedt were so effective that they helped the Wild finish last season with the fifth-best team save percentage in 5-on-5 play. What makes that detail important is the context that the Wild allowed the sixth-most scoring chances per 60 and allowed the seventh-most shots per 60. Only the Ducks allowed more in either category among playoff teams.

This season hinges on ... figuring out the depth given how much their roster has changed. Losing Marcus Johansson, Vladimir Tarasenko and Mats Zuccarello in the offseason means the Wild are without three of the players who finished in their top eight in points last season. GM Bill Guerin did reinforce the roster by bringing in Blake Coleman, with the belief that Maxim Shabanov and Danila Yurov can become significant contributors. Coleman is a proven scorer -- he has authored four seasons of more than 20 goals. Shabanov, who had 18 points in 44 games with the Islanders, will seek to find more consistency in his second season, while Yurov had 12 goals and 27 points as a rookie.

Most likely award winner: Quinn Hughes, Norris Trophy

Fantasy outlook: The Wild are one of the few squads with two top-20 forwards. Any manager who secures Kirill Kaprizov as a No. 1 and/or Matt Boldy as a No. 2 should count themselves fortunate. While Brock Faber won't put up as many points as Quinn Hughes, the 24-year-old blueliner provides his own value by blocking shots. -- Matiash

Bold prediction: Jesper Wallstedt is traded. -- Wyshynski

7. Montreal Canadiens
Last season: 48-24-10 (106 points), lost in conference finals

Stanley Cup odds: +2200

Projected points: 104.9

Biggest strength: The Canadiens' self-belief is a quality intangible that drove their unexpected run to an Eastern Conference final last year. And Montreal stuck to its guns by not doing much to reshape its roster -- putting full faith behind a vaunted core of Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Ivan Demidov, Lane Hutson and Juraj Slafkovsky (among others) to keep the good times going. The Canadiens ranked seventh in offense last year (averaging 3.40 goals per game) and they had a top-10 power play (at 23.1%) that elevated them from being potentially middle-of-the-pack to real players in the division (and, eventually, the conference at large). There is something to be said for consistency, and GM Kent Hughes' decision to run it back and let his team carry its momentum forward is an underrated asset that should benefit the Canadiens in the year ahead.

Biggest concern: There's another side to the offensive coin for Montreal. That is how the lack of alternations to the lineup could also sting -- particularly when it comes to scoring depth down the middle. Other than Hughes adding veteran Chris Kreider, this is essentially the same Canadiens team from a season ago. Good and bad. Because it remains true that after Suzuki -- the NHL's newly minted Selke Trophy winner -- there's a noticeable drop-off in talent at center. Oliver Kapanen and Jake Evans aren't touching Suzuki in terms of talent but they are primed to get more minutes than is optimal given Montreal's other options at the position. Michael Hage is in the pipeline but he's still cooking at the University of Michigan. It'll be internal candidates that Martin St. Louis has to choose from in ensuring Montreal can stack up to the competition at pivot.

This season hinges on ... whether goaltender Jakub Dobes is the real deal. Montreal certainly thinks so. And Dobes looked like a bona fide No. 1 when he took over last season from veteran Sam Montembeault to backstop Montreal's magical late-season push. It was the sort of showing that earns a three-year contract extension (like it did for Dobes) and the opportunity to enter this season as the team's go-to guy in the net. How well Dobes can wear that title -- and its accompanying workload -- will be an ongoing story for Montreal in this unprecedented 84-game season. Montembeault has been good in the preseason -- and will be pushing Dobes out of the gate. There's undeniable pressure on the 25-year-old to be Montreal's breakout star -- the calm, cool demeanor he kept on full display last spring, though, suggests he's comfortable with courting some spotlight.

Most likely award winner: Cole Caufield, Rocket Richard

Fantasy outlook: A rising young team with one of the league's most dangerous power plays. Juraj Slafkovsky is the target. The former No. 1overall pick came on strong (eighth overall in fantasy points from Dec. 1 onward) and is going a full round or two behind Nick Suzuki and Cole Caufield. -- Allen

Bold prediction: Lane Hutson is a Norris Trophy finalist. -- Wyshynski

8. Tampa Bay Lightning
Last season: 50-26-6 (106 points), lost in first round

Stanley Cup odds: +1000

Projected points: 113.1

Biggest strength: Tampa Bay is home to the NHL's reigning Hart Trophy winner -- that would be Nikita Kucherov -- and he headlines a top-end core of forwards that has kept the Lightning as contenders for most of the past decade. Brayden Point, Jake Guentzel, Brandon Hagel, Anthony Cirelli -- the list goes on of skaters who can instantly turn the tide in Tampa Bay's favor. The Lightning ranked fourth in offense last season, and though they faced some questions about being too top-heavy, when the talents are that strong, how can you not lean into them? That will be the case again this season for the Lightning. While Andrei Vasilevskiy's netminding has also been the (actual) backbone for Tampa Bay staying in contention, he's getting some seriously significant help from the Lightning's ability to deploy some of the league's best scorers.

Biggest concern: Tampa Bay isn't getting any younger. That's a real potential problem. The Lightning have excellent players at every position now pushing into their 30s -- Kucherov is 33, Victor Hedman is 35, Vasilevskiy is 32 -- and that's just to name a few. Experience is an undeniable asset and the Lightning have that in droves. But the NHL is increasingly injected with youthful skaters bringing speed and skill at rates we've never seen before and Tampa Bay has to keep up. The team relies so heavily on its old guard that when those players aren't at their best -- or available -- it shows in a profound way. Hedman, for example, appeared in only 33 games last season and the Lightning weren't the same without him. Coach Jon Cooper asks a good deal of Vasilevskiy in net and the toll that takes only increases with his age. Tampa Bay has made four consecutive first-round playoff exits looking like a tired team. Can the Lightning get back on form without some fresh blood?

This season hinges on ... how well the Lightning tune out noise surrounding Kucherov's impending path toward free agency. Tampa Bay's success runs through him -- and that's hardly hyperbole. Does the fact that Kucherov has so far refused to sign an extension suggest he's waiting to see how the Lightning do this season and decide whether there's enough hope they'll remain contenders for years to come? It's already apparent the Lightning could be approaching a period of transition given their overall age and the lack of recent postseason success. Somehow it feels like how the team responds to the cloud hanging over Kucherov will either unite it further or possibly create some discomfort that leaks onto the ice.

Most likely award winner: Nikita Kucherov, Ted Lindsay Award

Fantasy outlook: Elite and safe at the top, with Nikita Kucherov the league's most productive forward minute-for-minute. Watch the power-play battle: John Carlson's arrival threatens Hedman's return to key minutes, and with Victor Hedman now 35 and coming off a ton of missed time, that's the quarterback job to monitor. -- Allen

Bold prediction: Nikita Kucherov signs a new deal for less than $20M AAV. -- Wyshynski

9. Edmonton Oilers
Last season: 41-30-11 (93 points), lost in first round

Stanley Cup odds: +800

Projected points: 105.1

Biggest strength: Like the Avalanche, having two of the five best players on the planet -- in this case, Leon Draisaitl and Connor McDavid -- will always be a strong starting point. Centering their core around a pair of Hart Trophy winners is a strategy that has allowed the Oilers to entrench themselves as one of the major Western Conference powers. Yet that comes with the understanding that while winning the West is an accomplishment, this current group is still seeking an elusive Stanley Cup.

Biggest concern: Goaltending is a familiar concern for the Oilers. They had the second-worst team save percentage in 5-on-5 play last season. It's a continuation of the Oilers possessing a collective bottom-10 team save percentage in 5-on-5 play that goes back to the 2023-24 season. Signing Frederik Andersen and trading for Devon Levi gives them two more options beyond Tristan Jarry, who encountered his share of struggles after arriving in a trade last season. Also keep in mind that Andersen has had injury issues in his career, whereas Levi is still seeking to show how his AHL success can translate to the NHL.

This season hinges on ... all the moves they made this offseason leading to a title. The decision to hire Mike Babcock came after he was cleared by the NHL, following an investigation into what led to him resigning from the Blue Jackets -- including his request to look at the personal photos from players' phones. There was also the decision to sign Alex Formenton, the third of five players acquitted in the Hockey Canada sexual assault case that has signed with an NHL team. There are aforementioned concerns with Andersen and Levi, and hope that Ryan Shea can provide stability on the blue line. Pressure is mounting for the current group, given that McDavid's contract is up after 2027-28.

Most likely award winner: Connor McDavid, Hart Trophy

Fantasy outlook: Zach Hyman forecasts to bounce back after two mediocre/injury-riddled seasons. The veteran winger likes playing for Mike Babcock and seems fully fit after missing 24 games this past campaign. Evan Bouchard could eventually eclipse all fantasy blueliners if he ends up hitting the 100-point mark, as some optimistically anticipate. -- Matiash

Bold prediction: Mike Babcock makes no statistical difference for McDavid, Draisaitl. -- Wyshynski

10. Buffalo Sabres
Last season: 50-23-9 (109 points), lost in second round

Stanley Cup odds: +3000

Projected points: 86.2

Biggest strength: The Sabres have a laundry list of young players poised to make greater impacts with increased opportunity.
